hooks.text: The famous pigeon hero of World War I may have been misidentified.
Did Cher Ami really fly the Lost Battalion's message on October fourth?
Military records suggest the legendary pigeon's biggest flight was actually a different bird.

title: Cher Ami's True WWI Mission
description: Discover the surprising archival history behind Cher Ami, the famous homing pigeon of World War I.

beats.text: The famous pigeon hero of World War I may have been misidentified.
beats.visual: Rock pigeon wild type, Columba livia in urban habitat

beats.text: On October fourth, nineteen eighteen, the Lost Battalion was trapped in the Argonne Forest under heavy fire.
beats.visual: Argonne Forest France WWI battlefield landscape

beats.text: Major Charles Whittlesey wrote an urgent message asking to stop the friendly fire barrage.
beats.visual: General John J. Pershing WWI portrait

beats.text: Private Omer Richards released Cher Ami into the smoke-filled air to carry the plea.
beats.visual: WWI pigeon message capsule and carrier pigeon gear

beats.text: The brave bird flew twenty-five miles in just twenty-five minutes back to division headquarters.
beats.visual: Columba livia wild type homing pigeon in flight

beats.text: During that dangerous flight, Cher Ami was shot in the chest and nearly lost a leg.
beats.visual: French Croix de Guerre WWI medal close up

beats.text: Smithsonian curator Frank [Blazich](/blˈAzˈɪʧ/) notes official records show the wounding happened on a different mission entirely.
beats.visual: National Museum of American History interior exhibition Smithsonian
queries: National Museum of Natural History Washington

beats.text: DNA analysis also proved the bird was male despite early Signal Corps records listing him as a hen.
beats.visual: National Museum of Natural History Washington exterior
queries: National Museum of Natural History Washington
